title: What doesn't fit
hook: some things you met aren't for you

segments.voice: Yesterday, the schools you met, and one question: which way of practice drew you, and why? Your line was drawn to. Did that sentence get written down? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-three.

A book a friend lent you, its spine soft from years of rereading. They pressed it into your hands because it changed something for them. You have opened it again and again, and it will not open for you. You don't throw it away. You don't tell your friend it's a bad book. You hand it back, and say thank you. Yesterday was half of an honest look back: what drew you. Today is the other half. Some of what you met this year may not be for you. Maybe a chant that sounded like someone else's song. Maybe a sit that never opened. Maybe a thinker whose pages stayed shut. Today is about handing those back, kindly.
screen: `A BOOK THAT WON'T OPEN.` → `HAND IT BACK, WITH THANKS.` → `THE OTHER HALF OF THE LOOK BACK.`

segments.voice: First, not for me is not the same as not good. A practice that doesn't fit you is still whole for the people who keep it. A dawn prayer, a string of beads, a koan, an hour of silence: some people build their lives around each of them. Not for me is a sentence about me. It says nothing about the practice. Second, a teacher's picture. In The Prophet, Kahlil Gibran writes about what a real teacher does: "If he is indeed wise he does not bid you enter the house of his wisdom, but rather leads you to the threshold of your own mind." This year brought you to a great many houses. Not every one was meant to be moved into. Some were meant to be visited, admired and left, with the door closed gently behind you. Third, not for me can also mean not now. A book that won't open at one time of life sometimes opens at another. Letting something go kindly leaves the door unlocked. Letting it go with a sneer bolts it shut, and makes it harder to come back if you ever want to. Fourth, how to let go well. No mocking, no little story about how silly it was. Instead, name one thing it taught you, even if it's only what you don't need. A practice you set down can still have taught you something true about yourself. That's the thank-you note you tuck inside the cover when you hand it back.
screen: `NOT FOR ME IS NOT 'NOT GOOD'.` · `GIBRAN: THE THRESHOLD OF YOUR MIND.` · `NOT FOR ME CAN MEAN NOT NOW.` · `LET GO WITH THANKS.` · then, large: `NOT FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one thing go kindly. Settle, and let the breath be easy. Bring to mind one practice or idea from this year that didn't fit you. Don't argue with it, and don't argue with yourself. Just see it clearly, the way you'd look at a book on a friend's shelf. Then ask: what did it teach me, even a little? Let the answer be small. When you have it, set the thing down in your mind, the way you'd hand a borrowed book back to its owner. If you pray, you can give thanks for the people who keep it. The bell holds the time.
What doesn't fit. The practices and ideas from this year that aren't yours to keep, set down with respect for the people who do keep them. Today's word.
Your line: not for me. Today, if you catch yourself about to joke about someone else's way of practice, trade the joke for those three words, said kindly. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: People who try several practices may set some aside; doing it respectfully means not mocking the practice, and giving thanks for what it showed them.

notes: Gibran quotation (The Prophet, 'On Teaching', 1923) is from memory; confirm exact wording against the 1923 Knopf edition.
'Teachers in several traditions encourage doing so respectfully' in howItsDone is a general description; now softened to a plain description with no claim about teachers.

The lesson invites setting practices aside; confirm it never reads as dismissing any tradition, and that 'whole lives are built around' a dawn prayer, beads, a koan or silence is fair to each (now softened to 'some people build their lives around each').

Editor pass: the hook's borrowed coat became a borrowed book, because day 1415 had just used a clothes-fitting image (the shoe store); the coat image was carried through screen, teach, practice, match and myth and is now the book throughout; 'whole lives are built around each' softened; howItsDone no longer claims what teachers in several traditions encourage.
